items.title: Shocking Legal Win For Nigerian Woman Under Threat After Converting From Islam to Christianity
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A persecution watchdog is speaking out about a shocking case surrounding a Nigerian woman who scored a surprising legal victory after reportedly being detained and beaten for converting from Islam to Christianity.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Brad Brandon, CEO of Across Nigeria, recently returned from an extended trip to Nigeria, where he saw and experienced firsthand the horrific persecution impacing so many believers there. He joined CBN News to share that experience and to reflect on Sarah, the Nigerian woman whose court case is making international headlines.

“This is typically what happens,” he said of Sarah’s plight. “This happens, I mean … hundreds of times — thousands of times — a year in northern Nigeria. … 12 of the northern Nigerian states are controlled by Sharia law.”

Brandon said there’s a doctrine observed in many Muslim families there that a person who converts to Christianity has committed a crime – one that can sometimes be punishable by death. Sarah found herself in the crosshairs of this very dynamic.

“Your family can either kill you, or they can hire somebody to kill you, and that’s what’s going on in this case,” he said of Sarah. “So she converted to Christianity, and she felt threatened by her community and her family. She escaped that situation. Oftentimes, people will escape those situations with the help of other people.”

Sarah was in this camp as she found a Christian family to flee to after her siblings allegedly tried to force her into a marriage. The young woman stayed with this family, who helped rescue her and provide a safe haven; they were also reportedly involved in her conversion to Christianity.

As a result of their actions, the family also faces retribution.

“What they were accused of then is kidnapping,” he said. “And, again, all of these things, all of these details in this story, you could plug them into any other story. It’s the same thing that happens anywhere else.”

While a judge recently ruled in Sarah’s favor, deciding her rights were impeded when she was reportedly arrested, beaten, and mistreated for her conversion to Christianity, the family who helped her continues to face legal challenges.

items.title: Gang Members Violently Murder Christians, Torch Church
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: PRAY.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

At least 47 people and 22 others were injured Sunday night into Monday morning when gang members attacked a church providing shelter to displaced peoples right outside Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince.

The mayor of Kenscoff, Massillon Jean, said the deadly assault began around 10:30 p.m. and described it as a “night of terror.”

Jean blamed the Viv Ansanm gang coalition, one of the largest groups of violent gang members in Haiti.

According to an official statement, the Haitian government sent reinforcements to help local area police.

“Let there be no mistake: this time of mourning is also a challenge,” said the press release. “And to this challenge, the government responds with the force of law and the legitimate exercise of state force.”

It continued, “All security forces have been placed on maximum alert. Reinforcements are being deployed. The orders are clear: protect, secure, intervene. Government authority will be restored — firmly and without delay — throughout the entire territory of Kenscoff.”

The government added “no armed group will thrive in Haiti” and “[c]riminals will find no truce, no refuge, and no impunity.”

Haitian Bishop Joseph Gontrand Décoste of Jérémie told Aid to the Church in Need (ACN) that churches and Christians as a whole are increasingly the targets of gang violence because believers remain the last stalwart resistance against wrongdoing.

“We are the last remaining bulkhead — moral, ethical, spiritual, and prophetic,” he said. “That is why they want to eliminate us.”

For context, about 40 Catholic parishes have shut down in Port-au-Prince as Christians have faced increasingly deadly violence. In the first seven months of 2026, two priests were abducted and a seminarian was murdered. Last spring, two nuns from the Little Sisters of Saint Thérèse were killed and, in 2024, nine religious sisters, five brothers, and four priests were kidnapped.

ACN has reported gangs control somewhere between 70% and 90% of the capital city of Port-au-Prince.

items.title: Christ in Me
items.author: Jennifer Benson Schuldt
items.summary: Renaissance artist Albrecht Dürer became famous for his talent at age twenty. The art critics of his day called him “the greatest mind that ever expressed itself in line.” As his fame spread, influential people tried to hire him with promises of luxury and ease. Even other acclaimed
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Renaissance artist Albrecht Dürer became famous for his talent at age twenty. The art critics of his day called him “the greatest mind that ever expressed itself in line.” As his fame spread, influential people tried to hire him with promises of luxury and ease. Even other acclaimed artists such as Giovanni Bellini and Raphael revered his work.

In what experts consider to be his best self-portrait, Dürer mingled his physical characteristics with what he thought Jesus might have looked like. He painted himself with long wavy hair, a beard, and eyes that seemed to convey a sense of divine purpose. Many assumed this piece was a prideful statement about the artist’s opinion of himself. Others who were familiar with his virtuous character believed the painting wasn’t blasphemous or big-headed but aspirational. They believed Dürer wanted to live a life that would allow people to see Jesus in him.

If we truly know Christ, this is our desire as well. Believing in Him and accepting His death and resurrection as the basis for our relationship with God means we should now live for Jesus—not for ourselves (Galatians 2:19). We live for Him and He lives in us and works through us. The apostle Paul said this about his spiritual transformation: “I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (v. 20). May the glory of Christ shine through our lives today so that the world sees Him in us.

items.title: God’s Rich Provision
items.author: Patricia Raybon
items.summary: After Hurricane Helene’s floodwaters nearly destroyed his small North Carolina town in 2024, a pastor noticed an inspiring pattern. As he struggled to answer the persistent question, “What do you need?” donations kept showing up exactly when he needed them. Phone chargers? Out of t
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

After Hurricane Helene’s floodwaters nearly destroyed his small North Carolina town in 2024, a pastor noticed an inspiring pattern. As he struggled to answer the persistent question, “What do you need?” donations kept showing up exactly when he needed them. Phone chargers? Out of the blue, a man drove up with a generator, creating a charging station at the church. Drinking water? Suddenly, pallets of water bottles arrived.

Coincidence? The Bible points us to God, not mere happenstance. “My God will meet all your needs according to the riches of His glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19). The promise might seem empty to a town nearly demolished by a thirty-foot wall of raging water. But Paul, who was in prison when he offered this encouragement, was no stranger to hardship.

Paul was writing to the church in Philippi to thank them for badly needed financial gifts. Except for them, he’d been neglected (v. 15). But God used them to meet his needs. So, His words shined a bright light on God who provided the “riches of His glory” found in Christ Jesus our Savior, in whom we have “every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3). Joy, peace, truth, salvation are among the needs He richly provides. In kindness as well, He’ll provide a drink of water too, if that’s what we need. What a loving, generous God.

items.title: ‘I Don’t See How Revival Happens Without Prayer’: Philip Anthony Mitchell on the Three Things It’ll Actually Take
items.author: RELEVANT
items.summary: Philip Anthony Mitchell leads 2819 Church on Atlanta’s southwest side, a congregation named for Matthew 28:19, the verse where Jesus tells his followers to go and make disciples. He has led it under that name since January 2023, and in the three years since, it’s become one of the most c
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Philip Anthony Mitchell leads 2819 Church on Atlanta’s southwest side, a congregation named for Matthew 28:19, the verse where Jesus tells his followers to go and make disciples. He has led it under that name since January 2023, and in the three years since, it’s become one of the most closely watched churches in the country — packed rooms, millions of sermon views, a worship team with a label deal.

He won’t account for any of that. Mitchell calls the growth sovereign and says putting a formula to it would dishonor God. What he will talk about, at length and without hedging, is what he believes revival runs on.

“We have three pillars in our church,” he said. “Prayer, presence and proclamation.”

He doesn’t offer them as a model for other churches to copy. He offers them as prerequisites.

“I don’t see how revival happens without prayer,” Mitchell said. “I don’t see how revival happens without pure worship. And I don’t see how revival happens without Gospel preaching.”

The first is the least visible, and by his account it takes up most of the week.

“You put a camera on us during the week — we pray,” he said. “We wring out our heart from sin. We are striving for holiness and purity, and we just want to be faithful. We’re trying to do our part to show God that we can be trusted.”

The second is where Mitchell gets unusually specific for a lead pastor. While he doesn’t sing or appear on the church’s recordings, he sits in on songwriting anyway.

“I am a worshiper. And I think God has called us all to be worshipers,” he said. “Although I myself do not sing, I’m very passionate about music. I’m very passionate about worship. I’m very passionate about the sound of our house.”

That work runs through Trey Heflin, the church’s worship pastor, and through 2819 Worship, which signed with Reach Records. Mitchell has never tried to make the pairing make sense on paper. An album is expected in 2027.

“I want our worship to be pure, I want it to be holy, and I want the songs that we write to be born of the scriptures,” he said.

The third pillar is the one he frames as a fight. Mitchell wants the church to proclaim God’s word “unfiltered by all the things that have come to dilute God’s word,” and he is direct about what he thinks is doing the diluting.

“There is a generation right now that is emerging that is being led astray into counterfeit gospels,” he said. “And there is a Christianity in the West that is emerging that is disconnected from orthodox Christianity. And it burdens us. We cry, we weep about it.”

He knows how that lands. “It is countercultural,” he said. “We do take heat for that. But we are serious about what we’re doing.”

Underneath all three is a reading of the moment. Mitchell describes his church with a phrase from 1 Chronicles about the sons of Issachar, who understood their own times well enough to know what to do about them.

“We are sensitive to the times,” he said. “We believe that time is running out. The return of the Lord is near.”

That urgency is the reason he gives for most of what the church does, including the parts that sound like ambition from the outside. What he says he wants is narrower than a movement.

“Set aside all of our differences around color and ethnicity,” Mitchell said, “and be united around the last commandments of Christ — that His last commandments will be our first priorities.”

He describes the assignment as landing on everybody, in whatever room they’re already in: “from the single mom at home to the businessman in the Fortune 500 company to the athlete on the field.”

Heflin put the internal version of that plainly.

“We can’t be called a house that disciples or makes disciples and we not be disciples,” he said. “The moment that we find ourselves thinking that this is owed to us, the Lord will turn off that faucet of favor.”

He said the standard has to apply hardest to the people closest to the platform.

“We have to be just as serious as the single mom in the back that attends the church with four children, having to get up every morning,” Heflin said. “We have to be just as serious, if not more serious.”

Mitchell isn’t claiming 2819 has this figured out. Describing the staff culture, he stopped to say so.

“We are not perfect. And we have made mistakes,” he said. “But on this side of the camera, in full transparency, in terms of our staff, we are striving to be a people of holiness.”

He doesn’t offer any of it as an explanation for what is happening at 2819. Asked why people are coming en masse in recent years, Mitchell says only that it is sovereign.

“We plan like everything depends on us,” he said, “but we pray like everything depends on God.”

items.title: Sunday, August 30, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, last week we heard the great Gospel describing Peter’s confession.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Jeremiah 20:7-9

O Lord, you have enticed me,
    and I was enticed;
you have overpowered me,
    and you have prevailed.
I have become a laughingstock all day long;
    everyone mocks me.
For whenever I speak, I must cry out,
    I must shout, “Violence and destruction!”
For the word of the Lord has become for me
    a reproach and derision all day long.
If I say, “I will not mention him,
    or speak any more in his name,”
then within me there is something like a burning fire
    shut up in my bones;
I am weary with holding it in,
    and I cannot.

Psalm
Psalm 63:2, 3-4, 5-6, 8-9

So I have looked upon you in the sanctuary,
    beholding your power and glory.
Because your steadfast love is better than life,
    my lips will praise you.
So I will bless you as long as I live;
    I will lift up my hands and call on your name.
My soul is satisfied as with a rich feast,
    and my mouth praises you with joyful lips
when I think of you on my bed,
    and meditate on you in the watches of the night;
for you have been my help,
    and in the shadow of your wings I sing for joy.
My soul clings to you;
    your right hand upholds me.
But those who seek to destroy my life
    shall go down into the depths of the earth.

Second Reading
Romans 12:1-2

I appeal to you therefore, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your minds, so that you may discern what is the will of God—what is good and acceptable and perfect.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 16:21-27

From that time on, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and undergo great suffering at the hands of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “God forbid it, Lord! This must never happen to you.” But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me; for you are setting your mind not on divine things but on human things.”

Then Jesus told his disciples, “If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me. For those who want to save their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it. For what will it profit them if they gain the whole world but forfeit their life? Or what will they give in return for their life?

“For the Son of Man is to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay everyone for what has been done.

Reflection

Friends, last week we heard the great Gospel describing Peter’s confession. Because he says correctly who Jesus is, he is declared rock, the firm ground upon which the Church shall be built. And just moments later—our Gospel for today—he is told that he is a Satan, a stumbling block, thinking not as God thinks but as men think. What accounts for this rather remarkable reversal? 

In the Gospel, it’s always relatively simple: He doesn’t get the cross. The entire momentum of the life of Jesus is toward the cross. All sorts of forces are trying to keep him from it—some out of self-interest, some out of genuine concern. But they all have this in common: They don’t get it; they don’t get him.

So Peter, probably out of genuine love for Jesus, urges him away from the passion: “God forbid, Lord! No such thing shall ever happen to you.” Having correctly confessed who Jesus is, Peter promptly forgets what that entails. Being the Son of God, he thought, meant power and lordship, not ignominy and death.

items.title: The Passion of St. John the Baptist as a Witness to Marriage
items.author: Dr. Hannah Barrett
items.summary:
Dr. Hannah Barrett

John points to Christ by conforming himself to Christ’s death in the very reason for which John lays down his life. John dies for the dignity of marriage.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Hannah Barrett

On August 29, the Church celebrates the Memorial of the Passion of St. John the Baptist. It is striking that in the liturgical calendar the Church uses the same language only for John’s death as it does for Christ’s: a passion. John’s death is indeed a grim scene. The story, which is recounted in the Gospel reading of the day, loses none of its dramatic power from its familiarity. 

Herod lives with Herodias, the wife of Herod’s brother Philip, as if married. John publicly denounces the sin, provoking in Herodias a desire to kill him. She finds her opportunity when her husband is so pleased with her daughter’s dancing at his birthday banquet that he promises, “I will grant you whatever you ask of me, even to half of my kingdom.” Herodias pounces, having the girl request: “I want you to give me at once on a platter the head of John the Baptist.”

John dies because he refuses to let the sin of infidelity, on display by the powerful, go unnamed. His death, however, is more than the denouement of a story of moral outrage against one couple’s public sin. John’s death is a martyrdom. A martyr “bears witness to Christ who died and rose” (Catechism of the Catholic Church 2473). While St. Stephen is the first to die for Christ after the completion of Christ’s death and resurrection, and so is known as the protomartyr, St. John, as the forerunner of Christ, is at the forefront of the martyrs in the Roman Canon. In the Office of Readings for the day, Venerable Bede declares of John that “by his own suffering he showed that Christ also would suffer.”

But is John a martyr? Did his death bear witness to Christ’s death and resurrection, or did it just foreshadow it? Venerable Bede takes up this question:

There is no doubt that blessed John suffered imprisonment and chains as a witness to our Redeemer, whose forerunner he was, and gave his life for him. His persecutor had demanded not that he should deny Christ, but only that he should keep silent about the truth. Nevertheless, he died for Christ. Does Christ not say: I am the truth? Therefore, because John shed his blood for the truth, he surely died for Christ.

The Church reveres John’s memory because, in Bede’s words, “He stamped with the seal of martyrdom the testimony which he delivered on behalf of our Lord.” This testimony is deeper than one passion pointing to another. True, John’s passion points to Christ’s passion. But John points to Christ by conforming himself to Christ’s death in the very reason for which John lays down his life. In other words, John dies for the dignity of marriage. This is the doctrine for which he sheds his blood. In the Canticle of Zechariah, John’s father prophesies that John will go before the Lord “to give his people knowledge of salvation by the forgiveness of their sins.” Herod and Herodias are called to repent of their infidelity because repentance is the path to salvation; the way of the Lord is salvation itself, and this is what John prepares Israel for—first through his preaching of repentance and ultimately through his death in defense of marriage. Fidelity and forgiveness in marriage, John’s death insists, is itself a path to salvation. John’s rebuke of Herod is not merely a moral objection but a demanding teaching he enacts in his own unmarried flesh: Marriage is an arena in which spouses learn to die to self through the forgiveness of one another. John is the Church’s great defender of marriage. 

There is a still deeper layer beneath John’s defense of marriage, one that his own path through life was fashioned to disclose. St. John is the forerunner of Christ’s Passion; he is, uniquely among the martyrs, the one whose life and death prepared the way for the Lord’s death. He lived ascetically—a life of decrease—in order to point to the increase, the fullness, of Christ. The Gospel of John records his own account of this, given soon after Jesus’s first sign at the wedding at Cana: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice; therefore this joy of mine is now full. He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:27–30).

Read in this light, John’s passion is, subtly and wonderfully, a defense of Christ’s own mystical marriage to the Church. In defending the sign of marriage between man and woman, John defends the reality it signifies: the union of Christ and his Bride. He is the friend of the Bridegroom, and the friend of the Bridegroom lays down his life for his friend. His death is therefore a striking and unique profession of fidelity to Christ himself—a martyrdom that proclaims, in the very act of dying, the mystical marriage of Bridegroom and Bride, of Christ and his Church. This is the depth to which John is the friend of the Bridegroom: not merely an admirer pointing from afar, but a witness to Christ’s Passion by conforming himself to that Passion. Dying by defending the fidelity at the heart of marriage, John points in his death to Christ’s fidelity to the Church, laying down his life for his Bride. John’s is a martyrdom that witnesses “to Christ who died and rose” with a love as strong as death. The fidelity of Christ’s love for the Church makes sense of John’s death and makes possible a death-to-self fidelity in our own marriages.

At first glance, John dies for confronting the infidelity of Herod and Herodias. More profoundly, his death brings “knowledge of salvation” by defending marriage as a path of salvation. Even more profoundly, his martyrdom is a witness to Christ’s own mystical marriage to the Church, offered by the one who could call himself the Bridegroom’s friend. John’s passion is a sign to us of the path by which we become friends of the Bridegroom and by which our own marriages become signs of the marriage of Christ and his Bride: by a fidelity so serious, and a logic so strange, that we decrease—we die—so that Christ and his Bride—the union we become part of through this very way of salvation, this path of decrease—may increase.

St. John the Baptist, friend of the Bridegroom, defender of marriage, pray for us!
